lead: This unit explains how computers exchange data over wired and wireless links. After reading, you can identify network components, choose a topology, and map protocols to the correct layer.
about: The unit covers eight chapters. Chapter 1 (1.1) introduces data‑communication components and flow modes. Chapter 2 (1.2) classifies networks as LAN, MAN or WAN. Chapter 3 (1.3) describes common topologies. Chapter 4 (1.4) explains protocols, standards and the idea of layering. Chapter 5 (1.5) details the seven‑layer OSI model. Chapter 6 (1.6) presents the four‑layer TCP/IP suite and Internet architecture. Chapter 7 (1.7) contrasts circuit switching with packet switching. Chapter 8 (1.8) reviews network devices such as hubs, switches, bridges and routers. Each chapter builds on the previous one, moving from physical concepts to logical structures.

chapters.idea: Data communication moves bits from a source to a destination.
chapters.depth: Cover source, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination. Explain simplex, half‑duplex and full‑duplex modes. Some syllabi name these as direction of data flow.

figure.aria: Shows the five components of a data‑communication system and the direction of flow.

chapters.example: A sensor sends 500 bytes to a server over a 1 Mbps full‑duplex link. Transmission time = (500×8) bits ÷ 1 Mbps = 0.004 s.
chapters.trap: Counting both directions separately in full‑duplex and adding the time twice.
chapters.leave: Physical‑layer impairments are covered in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Networks are grouped by geographic reach.
chapters.depth: Define LAN (single building), MAN (city), WAN (nation or global). Give everyday examples such as a campus LAN, Chennai metro MAN, and a banking WAN. Some syllabi refer to these as network categories.

figure.aria: Nested sets illustrate that LANs are inside MANs which are inside WANs.

chapters.example: A college LAN uses 1 Gbps Ethernet, the city MAN uses 10 Gbps fiber, and the bank WAN uses 100 Mbps leased line. Total bandwidth if three sites connect via the WAN ≈ 11.1 Gbps.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the coverage area of LAN and MAN.
chapters.leave: Physical layout of links is discussed in Chapter 3.

chapters.depth: Describe bus, star, ring, mesh and tree topologies. Mention common uses such as Ethernet star and partial mesh in data centers. Some syllabi list these as network topologies.

figure.aria: Graph shows a star layout with a central switch and five end nodes, plus a few extra links for a partial mesh.

chapters.example: In a star of 5 computers each link is 100 Mbps. Maximum simultaneous traffic to the hub = 5×100 Mbps = 500 Mbps. A full mesh would have 10 links, total 1 Gbps.
chapters.trap: Using n×(n‑1) instead of n(n‑1)/2 for the number of mesh links.
chapters.leave: Layered protocol concepts continue in Chapter 4.

chapters.idea: Layers hide details and enable interoperability.
chapters.depth: Define protocol and standard. Explain why a layered model is used. Cite ISO, IEEE and IETF as standard bodies. Some syllabi call this protocol layering.

figure.aria: Three‑layer stack shows Application, Transport and Network layers.

chapters.example: Message "Hi" (2 bytes) passes down three layers. Each layer adds a 2‑byte header. Final frame size = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 bytes.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to add a header at one of the layers.
chapters.leave: Detailed OSI layer functions are covered in Chapter 5.

chapters.depth: List the layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Give a short function for each. Some syllabi refer to this as the OSI model.

figure.aria: Seven‑layer OSI model from Application down to Physical.

chapters.example: A TCP segment of 100 bytes gets a 20‑byte TCP header, a 20‑byte IP header and a 14‑byte Ethernet header. Size at Physical = 154 bytes.
chapters.trap: Placing Transport above Session or swapping the order of Data Link and Network.
chapters.leave: Mapping to the TCP/IP suite is done in Chapter 6.

chapters.idea: TCP/IP implements four layers for the Internet.
chapters.depth: Describe Application, Transport, Internet and Link layers. Map each to OSI layers. Mention IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP. Some syllabi call this Internet architecture.

figure.aria: Four‑layer TCP/IP stack with the Internet layer highlighted.

chapters.example: A web request uses HTTP over TCP over IPv4 over Ethernet. Payload 500 bytes, TCP header 20 B, IP header 20 B, Ethernet header 14 B. Total = 554 B.
chapters.trap: Assuming IPv6 header size is 20 B (it is 40 B).
chapters.leave: Switching concepts are introduced in Chapter 7.

chapters.idea: Two ways to move data through a network.
chapters.depth: Define circuit switching (dedicated path) and packet switching (shared links). Give telephone network vs Internet examples. Some syllabi label this as circuit vs packet.

figure.aria: Blocks compare a dedicated circuit path with a shared packet‑switching path.

chapters.example: A 64 kbps circuit is reserved for a 10‑minute call. Bits transmitted = 64 kbps × 600 s = 3.84 Mbits. In packet switching, five users share the same 64 kbps link, each averaging 20 kbps, causing queuing when total demand exceeds capacity.
chapters.trap: Treating packet switching as always faster than circuit switching without considering latency and congestion.
chapters.leave: Device‑level forwarding is covered in Chapter 8.

chapters.idea: Devices forward frames or packets based on different logic.
chapters.depth: Define hub (repeater), switch (MAC table), bridge (segment filter) and router (IP routing). Mention typical use cases such as home hub, office switch, campus bridge and ISP router. Some syllabi list these as network devices.

figure.aria: Block diagram shows data moving through a hub, switch, bridge and router from source to destination.

chapters.example: Host A sends a 1 MB file to Host D over a 100 Mbps switched LAN. Transmission time = (1 × 8 Mbits) ÷ 100 Mbps = 0.08 s, plus negligible switching delay.
chapters.trap: Assuming a hub amplifies the signal without creating a single collision domain.
chapters.leave: Routing algorithms are detailed in Unit 4.
